claim: Transcriptional gene silencing (TGS) can serve as an innate immunity against invading DNA viruses throughout Eukaryotes.
source: Transcriptional gene silencing (TGS) can serve as an innate immunity against invading DNA viruses throughout Eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a general statement about TGS function that draws from established scientific understanding of antiviral defense mechanisms.

claim: Geminivirus code for TrAP protein to suppress the TGS pathway.
source: Geminivirus code for TrAP protein to suppress the TGS pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Geminivirus biology referenced in the abstract.

claim: TrAP interacts with the catalytic domain of KYP.
source: TrAP interacts with the catalytic domain of KYP and inhibits its activity in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro pull-down assays and other biochemical experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: TrAP inhibits KYP activity in vitro.
source: TrAP interacts with the catalytic domain of KYP and inhibits its activity in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by the HMTase reconstitution assays presented in Figure 5.

claim: TrAP elicits developmental anomalies phenocopying several TGS mutants.
source: TrAP elicits developmental anomalies phenocopying several TGS mutants, reduces the repressive H3K9me2 mark and CHH DNA methylation, and reactivates numerous endogenous KYP-repressed loci in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations and molecular analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: TrAP reduces the repressive H3K9me2 mark in vivo.
source: TrAP elicits developmental anomalies phenocopying several TGS mutants, reduces the repressive H3K9me2 mark and CHH DNA methylation, and reactivates numerous endogenous KYP-repressed loci in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: TrAP reduces CHH DNA methylation in vivo.
source: TrAP elicits developmental anomalies phenocopying several TGS mutants, reduces the repressive H3K9me2 mark and CHH DNA methylation, and reactivates numerous endogenous KYP-repressed loci in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data presented in Figure 7.

claim: TrAP reactivates numerous endogenous KYP-repressed loci in vivo.
source: TrAP elicits developmental anomalies phenocopying several TGS mutants, reduces the repressive H3K9me2 mark and CHH DNA methylation, and reactivates numerous endogenous KYP-repressed loci in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KYP binds to the viral chromatin.
source: Moreover, KYP binds to the viral chromatin and controls its methylation to combat virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8I.

claim: KYP controls viral chromatin methylation to combat virus infection.
source: Moreover, KYP binds to the viral chromatin and controls its methylation to combat virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays and infection experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: kyp mutants support systemic infection of TrAP-deficient Geminivirus.
source: Notably, kyp mutants support systemic infection of TrAP-deficient Geminivirus.
evidence: This is supported by infection experiments and Southern blot analyses shown in Figure 9.

claim: TrAP attenuates the TGS of the viral chromatin by inhibiting KYP activity to evade host surveillance.
source: We conclude that TrAP attenuates the TGS of the viral chromatin by inhibiting KYP activity to evade host surveillance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: RNA silencing is a host defense mechanism to combat invading nucleic acids.
source: RNA silencing is a host defense mechanism to combat invading nucleic acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of plant-virus interactions.

claim: In PTGS, double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) are processed by Dicer-like ribonucleases into small-interfering RNAs (siRNAs).
source: In PTGS, double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) are processed by Dicer-like ribonucleases into small-interfering RNAs (siRNAs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PTGS pathway.

claim: Mature siRNAs are incorporated into an Argonaute (AGO)-centered RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) to regulate expression of target genes through RNA cleavage or translational repression.
source: Mature siRNAs are incorporated into an Argonaute (AGO)-centered RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) to regulate expression of target genes through RNA cleavage or translational repression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RISC mechanism.

claim: Virtually all plant viruses encode suppressor proteins that are able to block different key steps of the PTGS pathway.
source: To evade this surveillance mechanism, virtually all plant viruses are known to encode suppressor proteins that are able to block different key steps of the PTGS pathway (Ding and Voinnet, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Histone 3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) is mostly associated with transcriptionally active euchromatin.
source: The prevailing dogma is that histone 3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) is mostly associated with transcriptionally active euchromatin, while H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are repressive marks (Deal and Henikoff, 2011; Feng and Jacobsen, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are repressive marks.
source: The prevailing dogma is that histone 3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) is mostly associated with transcriptionally active euchromatin, while H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are repressive marks (Deal and Henikoff, 2011; Feng and Jacobsen, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: H3K9me2 is deposited by Arabidopsis Su(var)3-9 homolog 4, Kryptonite (KYP) and its paralogs (SUVH5,6).
source: Histone methylation is catalyzed by SET domain containing methyltransferases, specifically, H3K9me2 is deposited by Arabidopsis Su(var)3-9 homolog 4, Kryptonite (KYP) (Du et al., 2014a), and its paralogs (SUVH5,6), while H3K27 methylation is carried out by the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which includes Curly Leaf (CLF) (Liu et al., 2010; Zheng and Chen, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: H3K27 methylation is carried out by the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which includes Curly Leaf (CLF).
source: Histone methylation is catalyzed by SET domain containing methyltransferases, specifically, H3K9me2 is deposited by Arabidopsis Su(var)3-9 homolog 4, Kryptonite (KYP) (Du et al., 2014a), and its paralogs (SUVH5,6), while H3K27 methylation is carried out by the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which includes Curly Leaf (CLF) (Liu et al., 2010; Zheng and Chen, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In plants, KYP acts synergistically with DNA methyltransferases (i.e., Chromomethylase 3 [CMT3]) to constitute a mutually reinforcing cycle of DNA and histone methylation to secure TGS.
source: In animals, the propagation of histone methylation entails co-repressor heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1), whereas in plants, KYP acts synergistically with DNA methyltransferases (i.e., Chromomethylase 3 [CMT3]) to constitute a mutually reinforcing cycle of DNA and histone methylation to secure TGS (Du et al., 2012, 2014a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Plant DNA viruses, exemplified by Geminivirus, form minichromosomes in the host.
source: Plant DNA viruses, exemplified by Geminivirus, form minichromosomes in the host (Hanley-Bowdoin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Both Geminivirus DNA and associated histones are methylated in infected cells.
source: Both Geminivirus DNA and associated histones are methylated in infected cells, whereas viral methylation is reduced in methylation-deficient hosts, methylation-compromised Arabidopsis mutants are hypersusceptiple to Geminivirus infection and show exacerbated disease symptoms (Raja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Viral methylation is reduced in methylation-deficient hosts.
source: Both Geminivirus DNA and associated histones are methylated in infected cells, whereas viral methylation is reduced in methylation-deficient hosts, methylation-compromised Arabidopsis mutants are hypersusceptiple to Geminivirus infection and show exacerbated disease symptoms (Raja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Methylation-compromised Arabidopsis mutants are hypersusceptible to Geminivirus infection and show exacerbated disease symptoms.
source: Both Geminivirus DNA and associated histones are methylated in infected cells, whereas viral methylation is reduced in methylation-deficient hosts, methylation-compromised Arabidopsis mutants are hypersusceptiple to Geminivirus infection and show exacerbated disease symptoms (Raja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TrAP inhibits adenosine kinase (ADK).
source: It has been shown that TrAP inhibits adenosine kinase (ADK) (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: ADK catalyzes the synthesis of 5′ AMP from adenosine and ATP, a process that promotes the regeneration of S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM), the major methyl donor in the cell.
source: ADK catalyzes the synthesis of 5′ AMP from adenosine and ATP, a process that promotes the regeneration of S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM), the major methyl donor in the cell (Moffatt et al., 2002; Buchmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The TrAP-mediated inhibition of ADK activity likely impedes downstream trans-methylation events, including viral chromatin methylation in the nucleus.
source: Consequently, the TrAP-mediated inhibition of ADK activity likely impedes downstream trans-methylation events, including viral chromatin methylation in the nucleus (Bisaro, 2006; Buchmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations and logical inference.

claim: Some Geminivirus encode a TrAP positional homolog, named C2, that is able to stabilize SAM decarboxylase 1 to downregulate the methyl group metabolism.
source: In parallel, some Geminivirus encode a TrAP positional homolog, named C2, that is able to stabilize SAM decarboxylase 1 to downregulate the methyl group metabolism (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: C2 subverts the activity of COP9 signalosome to inhibit jasmonate signaling.
source: In addition, C2 also subverts the activity of COP9 signalosome to inhibit jasmonate signaling (Lozano-Durán et al., 2011), suggesting its multiple functions in viral counter-defense.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Constitutive expression of TGMV-TrAP in Arabidopsis thaliana caused morphological abnormalities that mimic loss-of-function mutants of numerous TGS components including lhp1 and clf.
source: We found that constitutive expression of TGMV-TrAP in Arabidopsis thaliana caused morphological abnormalities that mimic loss-of-function mutants of numerous TGS components including lhp1 (like-heterochromatin1) and clf.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Microarray analyses of TrAP transgenic plants and lhp1 mutants revealed a substantial overlap in reprogrammed host genes at a genome-wide level.
source: Microarray analyses of TrAP transgenic plants and lhp1 mutants revealed a substantial overlap in reprogrammed host genes at a genome-wide level.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: TrAP binds to the catalytic domain of KYP in vitro.
source: We demonstrated in vitro that TrAP binds to the catalytic domain of KYP and inhibits its enzymatic activity; while in vivo, TrAP decreases the repressive H3K9me2 marks and H3K9me2-dependent CHH methylation in gene-rich regions.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro pull-down assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: TrAP decreases the repressive H3K9me2 marks in vivo.
source: We demonstrated in vitro that TrAP binds to the catalytic domain of KYP and inhibits its enzymatic activity; while in vivo, TrAP decreases the repressive H3K9me2 marks and H3K9me2-dependent CHH methylation in gene-rich regions.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: TrAP decreases H3K9me2-dependent CHH methylation in gene-rich regions in vivo.
source: We demonstrated in vitro that TrAP binds to the catalytic domain of KYP and inhibits its enzymatic activity; while in vivo, TrAP decreases the repressive H3K9me2 marks and H3K9me2-dependent CHH methylation in gene-rich regions.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: KYP directly associates with the Geminivirus minichromosome.
source: We also found that KYP directly associates with the Geminivirus minichromosome and deposits H3K9me2 marks on viral chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8I.

claim: KYP deposits H3K9me2 marks on viral chromatin.
source: We also found that KYP directly associates with the Geminivirus minichromosome and deposits H3K9me2 marks on viral chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8G.

claim: kyp mutants but not wild-type plants sustain low systemic infection of CaLCuV lacking TrAP protein.
source: In addition, kyp mutants but not wild-type plants sustain low systemic infection of CaLCuV lacking TrAP protein.
evidence: This is supported by infection experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: KYP-catalyzed H3K9me2 is a line of the innate immunity against invading DNA pathogens.
source: Together with previous studies (Raja et al., 2008), we provide evidence that KYP evolves as a critical immune system to control invading nucleic acids in plants; this is reminiscent of the roles of human SUV39H1 in maintaining the latency of HIV (du Chene et al., 2007), Epsteinn-Barr virus (Imai et al., 2014), and some other mammalian viruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and supported by citations to related work.

claim: Geminivirus TrAP functions to inactivate KYP to counter host defense.
source: Thus, sequestering or interfering with this core component is an effective strategy for Geminivirus to block TGS and to subvert host defense; we expect this strategy to be used by other suppressors in plants and mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: 235 Arabidopsis transgenic lines overexpressing full-length TGMV TrAP were generated.
source: To study the suppression mechanism of TrAP, we generated 235 Arabidopsis transgenic lines overexpressing full-length TGMV TrAP, with or without Flag-Myc4, 3HA, or CFP epitopes.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The majority of TrAP transgenic lines exhibited developmental abnormalities consisting of short statures, strongly upward curled cotyledons and true leaves.
source: Importantly, the majority of the transgenic lines exhibited developmental abnormalities consisting of short statues, strongly upward curled cotyledons and true leaves (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TrAP overexpressing lines exhibited early flowering compared to wild-type plants.
source: Moreover, these overexpressing lines exhibited early flowering compared to wild-type (WT) plants.
evidence: This is a phenotypic observation from the transgenic plants.

claim: The phenotypes of TrAP transgenic plants were morphologically distinct from loss-of-function mutants of ADK1 ADK2, SnRK1, PEAPOD2, and rgsCaM.
source: These phenotypes were morphologically distinct from loss-of-function mutants of ADK1 ADK2 (Weretilnyk et al., 2001; Moffatt et al., 2002), SnRK1 (Shen et al., 2009, 2014), PEAPOD2 (Lacatus and Sunter, 2009), and rgsCaM (Chung et al., 2014), a calmodulin-like protein, which are also targets or partners of TrAP.
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The accumulation of miR165 and miR168 and their targets, PHB and AGO1 transcripts, in the 35S-TGMV TrAP lines was comparable to the amount in wild-type plants.
source: We observed that the accumulation of miR165 and miR168 and their targets, PHB and AGO1 transcripts, in the 35S-TGMV TrAP lines was comparable to the amount in wild-type plants (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA blot analyses shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Loading of miRNAs into AGO1-centered RISCs was not affected by TrAP.
source: We further confirmed that loading of miRNAs into AGO1-centered RISCs was not affected by TrAP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Unlike most previously reported viral suppressors, TrAP does not act on the miRNA pathway.
source: Thus, unlike most of previously reported viral suppressors, TrAP does not act on the miRNA pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the miRNA analysis experiments.

claim: 35S-TrAP transgenic lines phenocopied lhp1 mutants with respect to early flowering and upward curling of leaves.
source: We found that 35S-TrAP transgenic lines phenocopied several mutants in the epigenetic pathway including lhp1 (Kotake et al., 2003) (Figure 2A) and clf mutants (Chanvivattana et al., 2004), with respect to the early flowering and upward curling of leaves.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations and citations to previous work.

claim: 586 genes are differentially expressed in the 35S-TrAP transgenic plants (q < 0.005).
source: We examined global expression profiles of 7-day-old 35S-TrAP transgenic plants compared to Col-0 wild-type using an Affymetrix ATH1 GeneChip and identified 586 genes that are differentially expressed in the 35S-TrAP transgenic plants (q < 0.005).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Of the 586 differentially expressed genes in TrAP transgenic plants, 295 transcripts were elevated whereas 291 were reduced.
source: Of these, 295 transcripts were elevated whereas 291 were reduced (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Out of 295 genes significantly upregulated in the 35S-TrAP transgenic lines, 120 (40.7%) were also upregulated in lhp1 mutant.
source: Transcriptome analysis revealed that out of 295 genes significantly upregulated in the 35S-TrAP transgenic lines, 120 (40.7%) were also upregulated in lhp1 mutant.
evidence: This is supported by comparative microarray analysis shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The overlap of upregulated genes between TrAP transgenic lines and lhp1 mutant is significantly greater than expected by chance (p < 2.2e−16).
source: This is significantly greater than 1.28% expected by chance (p < 2.2e−16, Pearson's Chi-squared test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the microarray data.

claim: Out of 291 genes significantly downregulated in the 35S-TrAP transgenic lines, 137 (47.1%) were also repressed in lhp1 mutant.
source: Similarly, out of 291 genes significantly downregulated in the 35S-TrAP transgenic lines, 137 (47.1%) were also repressed in lhp1 mutant.
evidence: This is supported by comparative microarray analysis.

claim: The overlap of downregulated genes between TrAP transgenic lines and lhp1 mutant is significantly greater than expected by chance (p < 2.2e−16).
source: This is significantly greater than 1.25% expected by chance (p < 2.2e−16, Pearson's Chi-squared test) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the microarray data.

claim: Most of the tested transposons were transcriptionally active in TrAP transgenic plants.
source: Excitingly, most of the tested transposons were transcriptionally active (Figure 2I), further suggesting that TrAP indeed inhibits the TGS pathway, in both euchromatic and heterochromatic regions.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: LCI screening recovered LHP1 and KYP as proteins that interact with TrAP.
source: In our LCI screening, we recovered LHP1 and KYP, a SUVH-type H3K9me2 methyltransferase, suggesting that TrAP is physically close to LHP1 and/or KYP proteins in vivo (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by LCI assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TrAP co-localized with both LHP1 and KYP in scattered nuclear foci.
source: TrAP co-localized with both LHP1 and KYP in scattered but not yet clearly defined nuclear foci, whereas co-expression of TrAP-CFP and other YFP-tagged proteins in N. benthamiana cells did not show such patterns (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Co-IP assays validated the TrAP-KYP interaction but not TrAP-LHP1.
source: To further examine if TrAP interacted with these proteins, we conducted co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays (Figure 3D). Interestingly, we validated the TrAP-KYP interaction (Figure 3D) but not TrAP-LHP1 (data not shown), indicating that the LCI signal resulting from the TrAP-LHP1 combination likely involved additional cofactors between TrAP and LHP1 in vivo (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Only the full-length KYP showed specific interaction with TrAP in Co-IP assays.
source: We observed that expression of CLuc-HA3-KYP in N. benthamiana yielded truncated proteins of various lengths that accumulated to comparable levels as the full-length protein; only the full-length KYP showed specific interaction with TrAP, implying the KYP C-terminal domain as the interaction interface with TrAP (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: FRET-AB experiments confirmed TrAP-CFP/YFP-KYP interaction with positive FRET efficiency (CaLCuV-TrAP 2.699 ± 0.23, TGMV-TrAP 3.8228 ± 0.58, p < 0.05).
source: Consecutive cycles of YFP-KYP bleach/recovery correlated with release/quench on the TrAP-CFP signal (Figure 3E,F); the positive FRET-AB (CaLCuV-TrAP 2.699 ± 0.23, TGMV-TrAP 3.8228 ± 0.58, p < 0.05) corroborated TrAP-CFP/YFP-KYP interaction (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-AB experiments shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: A total of 624 peptides representing 288 unique sequences were recovered from the TrAP sample in mass spectrometry analysis.
source: A total of 624 peptides representing 288 unique sequences were recovered from the TrAP sample; of those, 31 unique peptides matched specifically to KYP/SUVH4 and were not found in control immunoprecipitates using Col-0 plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 31 unique peptides matched specifically to KYP/SUVH4 in the TrAP immunoprecipitate and were not found in control immunoprecipitates.
source: A total of 624 peptides representing 288 unique sequences were recovered from the TrAP sample; of those, 31 unique peptides matched specifically to KYP/SUVH4 and were not found in control immunoprecipitates using Col-0 plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MBP-KYP, but not MBP and other MBP-tagged control proteins, was able to pull down GST-tagged TGMV- and CaLCuV-encoded TrAP proteins in vitro.
source: We found that maltose-binding protein (MBP)-KYP, but not MBP and other MBP-tagged control proteins, was able to pull down GST-tagged TGMV- and CaLCuV-encoded TrAP proteins (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro pull-down assays shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: MBP-KYP was unable to pull down GST protein alone.
source: This interaction was specific as MBP-KYP was unable to pull down GST protein alone.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating specificity of the interaction.

claim: The SET domain of KYP interacted with TrAP proteins from both TGMV and CaLCuV at a higher affinity.
source: Pull-down assays showed that the SET domain interacted with TrAP proteins from both TGMV and CaLCuV at a higher affinity, whereas SRA domain might interact with CaLCuV TrAP at a reduced affinity in vitro (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro pull-down assays with truncated KYP proteins shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The SRA domain might interact with CaLCuV TrAP at a reduced affinity in vitro.
source: Pull-down assays showed that the SET domain interacted with TrAP proteins from both TGMV and CaLCuV at a higher affinity, whereas SRA domain might interact with CaLCuV TrAP at a reduced affinity in vitro (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro pull-down assays shown in Figure 4D-F, but the interaction is weaker.

claim: TrAP interacted with numerous tested HMTases (SUVH2, 5, and 6) in vitro.
source: In vitro pull-down assays showed that TrAP indeed interacted with numerous tested HMTases (SUVH2, 5, and 6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro pull-down assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Incubation of His-GST-KYP with His-MBP-TrAP from either TGMV or CaLCuV reduced the initial velocity of KYP transmethylation activity in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: Excitingly, incubation of His-GST-KYP with His-MBP-TrAP from either TGMV or CaLCuV reduced the initial velocity of KYP transmethylation activity in a dose-dependent fashion, whereas His-MBP alone did not affect KYP catalysis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro HMTase reconstitution assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: His-MBP alone did not affect KYP catalysis.
source: Excitingly, incubation of His-GST-KYP with His-MBP-TrAP from either TGMV or CaLCuV reduced the initial velocity of KYP transmethylation activity in a dose-dependent fashion, whereas His-MBP alone did not affect KYP catalysis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The TrAP-KYP molar ratio of 2 was enough to cause approximately 50% inhibition of KYP activity (IC50).
source: Quantification of signal intensity revealed that the TrAP-KYP molar ratio of 2 was enough to cause approximately 50% inhibition of KYP activity (half maximal inhibitory concentration [IC50]) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of HMTase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All tested loci in TrAP transgenic lines displayed consistent reduction of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3.
source: Remarkably, all tested loci in TrAP transgenic lines displayed consistent reduction of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, whereas changes of H3K4me3 were variable.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Changes of H3K4me3 in TrAP transgenic lines were variable.
source: Remarkably, all tested loci in TrAP transgenic lines displayed consistent reduction of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, whereas changes of H3K4me3 were variable.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The molecular phenotype of TrAP transgenic lines mimicked kyp mutant at all tested loci, but not lhp1 mutant.
source: This molecular phenotype mimicked kyp mutant at all tested loci, but not lhp1 mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP assay comparisons shown in Figure 6.

claim: Six out of seven TrAP deregulated loci including the flowering-promoting genes displayed greater than twofold reduction in H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 in the TrAP overexpression plants compared to wild-type Col-0.
source: Specifically, six out of seven TrAP deregulated loci including the flowering-promoting genes displayed greater than twofold reduction in H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 in the TrAP overexpression plants compared to wild-type Col-0, while changes in H3K4me3 were inconsistent.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: kyp mutant showed genome wide loss of methylation in CHG (∼42.1%) and CHH (∼21.7%), but not in CG (∼2%) contexts when compared to Col-0.
source: Consistent with previous studies, kyp mutant showed genome wide loss of methylation in CHG (∼42.1%) and CHH (∼21.7%), but not in CG (∼2%) contexts when compared to Col-0.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: TrAP transgenic plants only exhibited decrease in methylation of CHH (∼11%) but not CHG.
source: To our surprise, TrAP transgenic plants only exhibited decrease in methylation of CHH (∼11%) but not CHG (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: TrAP transgenic plants displayed loss of CHH methylation at gene-rich regions but not in TE-rich regions, nor in CG or CHG contexts.
source: When compared to Col-0, TrAP transgenic plants displayed loss of CHH methylation at GRR but not in TERR, nor in CG or CHG contexts (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of differentially methylated regions shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Of the 3442 and 1784 gene-rich region hypomethylated DMRs identified in kyp mutant and TrAP transgenic plants, 1642 were shared.
source: Remarkably, of the 3442 and 1784 GRR hypomethylated DMRs identified in kyp mutant and TrAP transgenic plants, 1642 were shared.
evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TrAP hypomethylated DMRs in coding sequences, UTRs, and introns overlapped almost completely with the kyp mutant (96.7%, 96%, and 95.4% respectively).
source: We found that TrAP hypomethylated DMRs in coding sequences, UTRs, and introns overlapped almost completely with the kyp mutant (96.7%, 96%, and 95.4% respectively) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: kyp mutants are hypersusceptible to Geminivirus infection.
source: Previous studies showed that kyp mutants are hypersusceptible to Geminivirus infection (Hanley-Bowdoin et al., 2013); these experiments were reproducible in our hands (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is supported by infection experiments shown in Figure 8A-D and citations to previous work.

claim: The hypersusceptibility of kyp mutant to the virus could be rescued by the wild-type KYP transgene under the control of both the native and the constitutive 35S promoters.
source: Moreover, the hypersusceptibility of kyp mutant to the virus could be rescued by the wild-type KYP transgene under the control of both the native and the constitutive 35S promoters (Figure 8A–D); further validating a role for KYP in regulation of viral infection.
evidence: This is supported by complementation experiments shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: Wild-type KYP almost completely rescued H3K9me2 defects of the TEs in the kyp mutant.
source: In line with the phenotypic complementation, wild-type KYP almost completely rescued H3K9me2 defects of the TEs in the kyp mutant (Figure 8E, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8E.

claim: H3K9me2 marks were dramatically decreased on several, but not all tested loci in the viral genome in kyp mutant.
source: Interestingly, H3K9me2 marks were dramatically decreased on several, but not all tested loci in the viral genome in kyp mutant, and the methylation marks were further restored by the KYP transgene, suggesting that viral chromatin H3K9me2 is catalyzed by KYP.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The methylation marks on viral chromatin were restored by the KYP transgene.
source: Interestingly, H3K9me2 marks were dramatically decreased on several, but not all tested loci in the viral genome in kyp mutant, and the methylation marks were further restored by the KYP transgene, suggesting that viral chromatin H3K9me2 is catalyzed by KYP.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8G.

claim: KYP was found at all tested loci in the viral chromatin in ChIP assays.
source: Excitingly, KYP was found at all tested loci in the viral chromatin (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays using anti-Flag antibody shown in Figure 8I.

claim: CaLCuV-infected plants showed 60–100% H3K9me2 loss in the tested loci compared to the amount in the mock-inoculated plants.
source: CaLCuV-infected plants showed 60–100% H3K9me2 loss in the tested loci compared to the amount in the mock-inoculated plants (Figure 8E), this is reminiscent of the molecular phenotype of TrAP transgenic plants, which showed lower enrichment of H3K9me2 mark at the studied loci (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assays shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Wild-type plants did not show any symptoms of infection or systemic accumulation of CaLCuV Δtrap.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the wild-type plants did not show any symptoms of infection (Figure 9E) or systemic accumulation of CaLCuV Δtrap, as evidenced by Southern blot analyses and PCR (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by infection experiments, Southern blot, and PCR analyses shown in Figure 9C and E.

claim: Viral DNA was detected, in low amount but reproducibly, in kyp mutants infected with CaLCuV Δtrap.
source: Excitingly, the viral DNA was detected, in low amount but reproducibly, in kyp mutants.
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot and PCR analyses shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: PCR amplification of the TrAP gene followed by XbaI digestion confirmed that the detected viral DNAs in kyp mutants indeed came from CaLCuV Δtrap and not from a reversion of the mutation in the virus genome.
source: Further PCR amplification of the TrAP gene followed by XbaI digestion, confirmed that the detected viral DNAs in kyp mutants indeed came from CaLCuV Δtrap and not from a reversion of the mutation in the virus genome.
evidence: This is supported by PCR and restriction digestion analyses shown in Figure 9D.

claim: kyp plants sustained systemic infection of CaLCuV Δtrap.
source: These results show that kyp plants sustained systemic infection of CaLCuV Δtrap.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the infection experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: The titers of accumulated CaLCuV Δtrap were much lower than the ones of CaLCuV.
source: Noticeably, the titers of accumulated CaLCuV Δtrap were much lower than the ones of CaLCuV, suggesting either redundant activity of KYP paralogs in host defense or necessity of additional functions of TrAP besides inhibition of KYP activity for the virus to achieve efficient infection.
evidence: This is an observation from the infection experiments shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Direct inhibition of KYP represents a novel counter-defense mechanism for virus survival in the hosts.
source: Thus, direct inhibition of KYP represents a novel counter-defense mechanism for virus survival in the hosts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: This mechanism could account for the long-documented essential role of TrAP in expression of viral genes including the coat protein and the nuclear shuttle protein.
source: This mechanism could account for the long-documented essential role of TrAP in expression of viral genes including the coat protein and the nuclear shuttle protein (Sunter and Bisaro, 1992; Yang et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2009; Hanley-Bowdoin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis connecting the findings to previous knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: In plants, H3K9me2 marks often correlate with non-CG DNA methylation, and in particular with CHG modification.
source: In plants, H3K9me2 marks often correlate with non-CG DNA methylation, and in particular with CHG modification.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epigenetic regulation in plants.

claim: The tight coordination between H3K9me2 and CHG methylation results from a self-enforcing loop consisting of KYP and CMT3.
source: The tight coordination results from a self-enforcing loop consisting of KYP and CMT3 (Du et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: KYP methylates H3K9 to generate the binding sites for CMT3, which further methylates CHG DNA to create more binding sites for KYP.
source: Briefly, KYP methylates H3K9 to generate the binding sites for CMT3, which further methylates CHG DNA to create more binding sites for KYP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the KYP-CMT3 feedback loop.

claim: Methylation in the CHH context is catalyzed by CMT2 and DRM1/2 in Arabidopsis.
source: Methylation in the CHH context is catalyzed by CMT2 and DRM1/2 in Arabidopsis, and the sites regulated through the two sets of enzymes are mostly non-overlapping.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA methylation pathways.

claim: The sites regulated through CMT2 and DRM1/2 are mostly non-overlapping.
source: Methylation in the CHH context is catalyzed by CMT2 and DRM1/2 in Arabidopsis, and the sites regulated through the two sets of enzymes are mostly non-overlapping.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA methylation pathways.

claim: The functions of CMT2 and DRM1/2 are mostly non-redundant at CHH sites.
source: Thus, the functions of CMT2 and DRM1/2 are mostly non-redundant at CHH sites (Stroud et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DRM1/2 largely catalyze CHH methylation at the TE-rich regions.
source: DRM1/2 largely catalyze CHH methylation at the TE-rich regions (Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Bulk CHH methylation is maintained by CMT2.
source: Importantly, it has been recently discovered that bulk CHH methylation is maintained by CMT2 (Shen et al., 2014; Stroud et al., 2014; Dubin et al., 2015) and that its activity is largely dependent on H3K9me2.
evidence: This is recent knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CMT2 activity is largely dependent on H3K9me2.
source: Importantly, it has been recently discovered that bulk CHH methylation is maintained by CMT2 (Shen et al., 2014; Stroud et al., 2014; Dubin et al., 2015) and that its activity is largely dependent on H3K9me2.
evidence: This is recent knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CMT2 recognizes methylated H3K9 but preferentially binds to di-methylated over mono-methylated histone tails.
source: In this scenario, CMT2 recognizes methylated H3K9 but preferentially binds to di-methylated over mono-methylated histone tails.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CMT2 specificity.

claim: This preference towards H3K9me2 is not observed in the CHG methyltransferase CMT3, which can equally bind to all forms of H3K9 methylation.
source: This preference towards H3K9me2 is not observed in the CHG methyltransferase CMT3, which can equally bind to all forms of H3K9 methylation (Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Geminivirus DNAs undergo extensive methylation modification in the host.
source: In the host, Geminivirus DNAs also undergo extensive methylation modification (Raja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The Geminivirus replicase, Rep/AC1/C1 and the embedded protein AC4/C4, downregulate the expression of host DNA methyltransferases MET1 and CMT3.
source: Remarkably, the Geminivirus replicase, Rep/AC1/C1 and the embedded protein AC4/C4, downregulate the expression of host DNA methyltransferases MET1 and CMT3 (Pumplin and Voinnet, 2013; Rodriguez-Negrete et al., 2013); hence, it interrupts the reinforcing loop of histone and DNA methylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: cmt3 mutants exhibit hypersusceptibility to viral infection.
source: Consistent to this study, cmt3 mutants exhibit hypersusceptibility to viral infection (Raja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Arabidopsis has 49 SET domain containing proteins of which 31 are considered to have HMTase activity.
source: We note, however, that Arabidopsis has 49 SET domain containing proteins of which 31 are considered to have HMTase activity (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: H3K27me3 and LHP1-bound sites are predominantly distributed in the euchromatic regions.
source: Interestingly, recent ChIP–chip studies revealed that H3K27me3 and LHP1-bound sites are predominantly distributed in the euchromatic regions (Turck et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007a, 2007b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: KYP-dependent H3K9me2 marks are highly enriched at pericentromeric regions as large and uninterrupted heterochromatic blocks.
source: This distribution is not correlated with KYP-dependent H3K9me2 marks that are highly enriched at pericentromeric regions as large and uninterrupted heterochromatic blocks (Liu et al., 2010; Black et al., 2012; Du et al., 2014a; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: H3K9me2 can also occur in euchromatic regions but rather exist as small heterochromatin patches.
source: H3K9me2 can also occur in euchromatic regions but rather exist as small heterochromatin patches (Zheng and Chen, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Human SUV39H1 plays a role in maintaining the latency of HIV.
source: Together with previous studies (Raja et al., 2008), we provide evidence that KYP evolves as a critical immune system to control invading nucleic acids in plants; this is reminiscent of the roles of human SUV39H1 in maintaining the latency of HIV (du Chene et al., 2007), Epsteinn-Barr virus (Imai et al., 2014), and some other mammalian viruses.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Human SUV39H1 plays a role in maintaining the latency of Epstein-Barr virus.
source: Together with previous studies (Raja et al., 2008), we provide evidence that KYP evolves as a critical immune system to control invading nucleic acids in plants; this is reminiscent of the roles of human SUV39H1 in maintaining the latency of HIV (du Chene et al., 2007), Epsteinn-Barr virus (Imai et al., 2014), and some other mammalian viruses.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TrAP is a potent inhibitor of HMTase activity.
source: Our KYP reconstitution assays show that TrAP:KYP molar ratio of around 2 is enough to cause ∼50% inhibition of KYP activity, indicating that TrAP is a potent inhibitor of HMTase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro HMTase assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: TrAP does not target the HMTases that are writers for the active marks such as H3K4me3 and H3K36me3.
source: Notably, we did not observe the repression of transcriptionally active histone methylation marks, such as H3K4me3 and H3K36me3. This observation suggests that TrAP does not target the HMTases that are writers for the active marks.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that active histone marks were not affected by TrAP.
